subject: Culture
title: Hagia Sophia's Identity
description: Learn Hagia Sophia's Identity in one minute.

hook.text: Hagia Sophia was a church for 916 years, a mosque for 481 years, a museum for 86 years, and a mosque again since 2020.

buildup.text: Emperor Justinian built it in 537 AD. When he entered he reportedly said: 'Solomon, I have surpassed thee.'

discovery.text: After the Ottoman conquest in 1453, minarets were added. Christian mosaics were plastered over but not destroyed.

twist.text: Atatürk made it a museum in 1934 to signal secular modernity. Erdoğan reversed it to signal Islamic identity.

climax.text: Both actions used the same building to broadcast competing visions of Turkey—and both worked.

punchline.text: A building can change religions without moving a single stone.

details.summary: Hagia Sophia in Istanbul has been a Christian cathedral, an Ottoman mosque, a secular museum, and a mosque again — all within the same breathtaking structure. Its identity changes reflect 1,500 years of religious and political power struggles over one of the world's most magnificent buildings.
details.whyItMatters: Hagia Sophia embodies the clash between preservation and possession of sacred spaces. Its conversions reveal how conquering powers use architecture to claim spiritual authority over the defeated.
takeaways: Hagia Sophia was the world's largest cathedral for nearly 1,000 years
It became a mosque after Ottoman conquest in 1453
Turkey reconverted it from a museum to a mosque in 2020

faq.question: Why is Hagia Sophia so architecturally significant?
faq.answer: Built in 537 CE under Emperor Justinian, its massive dome (31 meters across) was an engineering marvel that remained unsurpassed for nearly a millennium. The dome appears to float on a ring of windows, filling the interior with light.

faq.question: Why was Hagia Sophia's reconversion to a mosque controversial?
faq.answer: Turkey converted the museum back to a mosque in 2020, sparking international debate. Critics argued it reversed Atatürk's secular legacy and threatened Byzantine mosaics. Supporters said Turkey had sovereign right over its heritage and that mosques can coexist with historical art.
